messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Librarian
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence, Event Involvement: People who are related to the event, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mai Tran was fifty-two, a librarian in a small coastal town, when she finally made an appointment with a trauma specialist. The event that had upended her life occurred four years earlier. Typhoon Ketsana had struck without warning one autumn night. Mai was alone in her ground-floor apartment; the power failed, plunging her into complete darkness as floodwater rose past her knees. The worst part came after the winds died down. A sudden, profound silence settled—no rain, no wind, just the lapping of water and her own ragged breaths. When daylight came, she learned that a neighbor, a woman she had spoken to the day before, had drowned in the same flood. Mai had not heard a thing; the silence had masked the neighbor’s cries.

In the months that followed, the memory of that night began forcing its way into her mind without warning. Something as simple as a library patron falling silent while reading could instantly return her to the dark, to the cold water, and to the crushing grief she had felt upon learning of her neighbor’s death. That grief—overwhelming, fresh—would hit her mid-shelf, and she would have to brace herself against the bookcase. The silence itself had become a trigger, and she found herself scanning every quiet room for exits, for things that might suddenly go wrong. Every time the reading room fell still, her vigilance sharpened: she would grip the desk, her eyes darting from corner to corner, certain that something terrible was about to happen again.

This hypervigilance only made the intrusions worse. The more she watched for danger in the dark, the more the memory would surge back—untethered, uncontrolled. She began to experience the memory as a threat in its own right, so that even recalling the event would put her on edge, sending her scanning for signs of the kind of sudden change that had preceded the typhoon. Darkness, especially, became a signal: if she woke in the night, even to use the bathroom, the absence of light would trigger the full sensory replay—the water, the silence, the grief—and she would lie rigid, convinced she heard water seeping under the door. That fear, in turn, made nighttime a trigger she could not escape.

Mai developed strategies to manage. She deliberately tried to leave her body or blank out when the intrusions came—a kind of mental dissociation that she hoped would stop the images. But instead, the effort to escape often brought the memory closer, as though her mind was fighting back. She also began to avoid anything that reminded her of the event: she stopped walking through the park after work because the dusk felt too close to dusk on the day of the storm; she would not exercise at all, even though she had once been an avid walker, because physical exertion made her breathless, and that feeling of being out of breath took her straight back to the water. In the library, she always chose the chair in the corner of the staff room, where she could see both doors and no one could approach from behind. She needed to feel safe, and that need dictated where she sat.

Avoiding the dark meant she went home before sunset, curtailing her social life and drawing sharp questions from her husband. He did not understand why she had become so jumpy, why she flinched when he walked into a room silently. Mai could not explain. The silence itself had become a trigger, and when she was confronted with it, her only option was to dissociate—to go elsewhere, inside her head, until the danger passed. Yet trying to dissociate often caused the memory to intrude more forcefully, as though her mind was punishing her for trying to escape. And each time she avoided a circumstance, such as being in the dark, that very avoidance made the trigger feel larger, more looming, more certain to cause harm the next time she could not avoid it.

She first realized she needed help when a visiting scholar asked her a question in the reading room, and Mai could not respond. The library had fallen into one of those sudden silences, and she had frozen, scanning the tables, waiting for something to happen. The scholar’s voice came from far away, but Mai was back in the dark water, full of grief. When she came to, she had left her body for a moment—blanked out entirely. The fact that it happened at work, in front of a patron, horrified her. She made the appointment the next day. What frightens her most now is the prospect of being trapped in silence again, unable to escape her own memory. She hopes, deep down, that talking will somehow break the loop—that she can learn to hear quiet without feeling the flood rise around her.
